Galley-Slave Pastors
gal'i-slav pas'torz
n. pl. (the Hungarian Protestant ministers and schoolmasters condemned in 1674 and sent to the Naples galleys, released in February 1676)
Galley, from Late Latin galea, an oared warship; the Hungarian name galyarab prediktorok, galley-slave preachers, is the title under which they are remembered.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Of the hundreds of Hungarian Lutheran and Reformed ministers and schoolmasters cited before the Pozsony tribunal in 1673 and 1674, a remnant would neither convert nor resign nor accept exile. Some were held in fortress prisons; about forty were sent south in the spring of 1675, driven on foot across Styria and the Italian states in chains, shown in the towns as condemned criminals, and sold to the Spanish galley fleet at Naples. Several died on the road and several at the oar. Their case became known in Protestant Europe through letters smuggled out and through the Dutch and Swiss churches, and the Dutch Republic took it up as a matter of state. In February 1676 the admiral Michiel de Ruyter, then in the Mediterranean, demanded and obtained the release of the twenty-six survivors, took them aboard, and landed them at Naples a free company; they made their way to Venice, Zurich and the German universities, and a few lived to return to Hungary after the Diet of Sopron. Their narratives were printed and read for two centuries. The dictionary enters them as the clearest instance in the whole period of a refusal that cost everything and conceded nothing: men who were offered their liberty, their livings and their homes for a signature, and who did not sign.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a galley-slave as a person condemned to work at the oar; a confessor as one who makes profession of his faith under persecution; and ransom as the release of a captive by paying a price.

expand to see more

GALLEY-SLAVE, n. A person condemned for a crime to work at the oar on board of a galley; hence, one in the lowest condition of servitude.

CONFESSOR, n. One who makes a profession of his faith in the Christian religion; one who avows his religion in the face of danger.

RANSOM, n. [L. redemptio.] The money or price paid for the redemption of a prisoner or slave, or for goods captured by an enemy.

CHAIN, n. [L. catena.] A series of links or rings connected; that which binds; a bond; fetters; hence, bondage, slavery.

DELIVERANCE, n. Release from captivity, slavery, oppression or any restraint; rescue from danger or any evil.

Key Scripture

Psa 107:10 — "Such as sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, being bound in affliction and iron;"

Heb 13:3 — "Remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them; and them which suffer adversity, as being yourselves also in the body."

Psa 102:20 — "To hear the groaning of the prisoner; to loose those that are appointed to death;"

Act 16:25 — "And at midnight Paul and Silas prayed, and sang praises unto God: and the prisoners heard them."

Modern Corruption

The Hungarian ministers who refused to convert, resign or go into exile, were sold to the Naples galleys in 1675, and were freed by a Dutch admiral in 1676.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the devotional one: the story told as a tale of heroism with the alternative left out. The alternative is what makes it a confession. These men were not seized at random; each was offered a document and could have gone home. The dictionary states the terms plainly, because a reader who does not know what was on the table cannot see what was refused, and because the same offer is made in every generation in some milder currency.

The principle to recover is the church's duty to prisoners. “Remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them” (Heb 13:3) was obeyed here by the Dutch and Swiss churches, who did not merely pray but wrote, printed, petitioned and at last used a fleet. Intercession that never becomes action is not what the text asks. The dictionary also records the honour of de Ruyter, a plain Reformed seaman who thought the release of twenty-six Hungarian preachers a proper use of a Dutch squadron.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew asir (H615), a prisoner, one bound; Hebrew anaqah (H603), a groaning or sighing.

Hebrew choshek (H2822) — darkness; “Such as sit in darkness and in the shadow of death”, Psalm 107:10.

Hebrew barzel (H1270) — iron, fetters of iron; “being bound in affliction and iron”, Psalm 107:10.

Greek desmios (G1198) — a prisoner, one in bonds; “Remember them that are in bonds”, Hebrews 13:3.

Hebrew anaqah (H603) — a groaning, a sighing; “To hear the groaning of the prisoner”, Psalm 102:20.

Greek humneo (G5214) — to sing a hymn, to praise in song; “Paul and Silas prayed, and sang praises unto God”, Acts 16:25.

Usage

"“being bound in affliction and iron” (Psa 107:10) — driven on foot to Naples in chains in the spring of 1675."

"“Remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them” (Heb 13:3) — the Dutch and Swiss churches, who petitioned and then sent a fleet."

"“To hear the groaning of the prisoner; to loose those that are appointed to death” (Psa 102:20) — twenty-six survivors freed in February 1676."
